newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan Inc may see more victims of bubble-era debt.
newsitem.headline: Japan Inc may see more victims of bubble-era debt.

text.p: Fears are growing that Japan Inc will see more victims from the excesses of its "bubble" era, possibly in the troubled construction sector, as banks become increasingly willing to let firms go under, analysts say.

Shares of some construction firms burdened with massive bubble-era loans tumbled to their lowest level ever on the Tokyo bourse on Friday as concerns over their financial health led to heavy waves of selling.
The market as a whole managed to cling on to gains with the benchmark Nikkei 225 average rising by 120.71 points or 0.61 percent to end at 19,875.49.
"A sense of tragedy, more than a mere negative feeling, is prevailing in the construction sector," said Keiko Otsuki, an analyst at UBS Securities Ltd in Tokyo.
Brokers said medium-sized general contractors Aoki Corp and Tada Corp saw heavy sales, along with Japanese retailer Yaohan Japan Corp, which also has debt problems.

Aoki Corp dove to a record low of 64 yen on Friday before closing the day down 16 yen at 84, spurred by concern over its slow progress in reducing its interest-bearing debt worth some 326.9 billion yen ($2.86 billion).
Shares of Tada Corp, meanwhile, closed at a record low of 115 yen.

Brokers said that worries over construction firms buckling under the weight of bad loans, a legacy of the asset price bubble in the 1980s, intensified after news last week that general contractor Tokai Kogyo Co Ltd had applied for court protection. Tokai Kogyo is the first listed general contractor to ever go under.
"The construction sector is the Achilles' heel of the stock market," a "Big Four" broker said.

Japan's construction sector now has some 10 trillion yen ($87.7 billion) worth of interest-bearing debt, and a likely rise in domestic interest rates may make it hard for some firms in the sector to pay interest to banks, analysts said.

"A possible rise in interest rates and the introduction of an early warning system (by the Finance Ministry) led to a view that banks may prefer to let troubled firms go under in order to clean up their balance sheets," UBS's Otsuki said.

"With interest rates seen edging up, public spending falling and if the economy doesn't recover, several firms may be in danger," Otsuki said, adding that over ten firms in the sector are now in bad shape in terms of adjusted book value per share, a key gauge of financial health. He said their fate hinges on how their creditor banks act.
A fall in share prices on Friday forced Aoki president Yoichiro Yano to call a news conference to reassure the market that its business was going well.

"Our business is moving steadily and we have no problems," Yano said. He said Aoki could be profitable even if domestic interest rates were to be raised by 0.5 percentage point as expected by market players.

Similar attempts by retailer Yaohan Japan to convince investors that it is in strong financial health were not convincing. Yaohan's shares were haunted by worries that it may not be able to repay its creditors, although the firm denied rumours that it was considering seeking court protection from creditors in an evening news conference on Thursday.
Yaohan's shares briefly fell by the daily limit to 93 yen on Friday afternoon, after having been ask-only for most of the session, and ended the day 48 yen weaker at 95, a record closing low.
"Market participants are sifting through shares, separating the good from the bad," said Tadahiro Kamogawa, Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd's general manager.

Few market participants, however, believe the jitters will drag the whole stock market down as unlike the situation late last year, market sentiment is not bleak and investors do not feel compelled to reduce their stock holdings.

"The shares of firms which are seen having problems are being sold, but there is a view that such problems are isolated cases and are not of the proportion that would drive the entire market lower," Yamaichi's Kamogawa said.
